book.title: Blink: The Power of Thinking Without Thinking
book.author: Malcolm Gladwell

confidence_note: The Warren Harding Error is a chapter-level idea in Blink. Gladwell describes how the political operator Harry Daugherty met Harding around 1899 in Ohio and was struck by how presidential he looked; Harding's handsome appearance and resonant voice helped carry him to the presidency in 1920, and he is widely rated one of the worst presidents; he died in office in 1923. The reference TR text's summary is broadly correct. Gladwell's broader point is kept: snap judgments can be distorted by stereotypes and associations, as in the Harding case, and the book discusses studies showing tall men are overrepresented among CEOs; exact percentages are omitted.
facts: Around 1899, Harry Daugherty, an ambitious Ohio political operator, met Warren Harding and was struck by how much he looked like a president.
Harding was tall, handsome, with a deep voice and a dignified manner. He was not especially intelligent or accomplished, but his appearance helped his political rise.
With Daugherty's backing, Harding became a senator and then won the presidency in 1920.
He is widely considered one of the worst presidents in American history. He died in office in 1923.
Gladwell calls this the Warren Harding Error: a snap judgment triggered by appearance or association rather than by the qualities that matter.
He contrasts it with expert thin-slicing: fast judgments can be brilliant, but they can also be corrupted by stereotypes and unconscious bias.
As another example, Gladwell notes that tall men are heavily overrepresented among the CEOs of large companies.
tension: The same quick judgment that saves a fire crew can also put the wrong man in the White House.
opening_idea: A man looks so much like a president that people make him one.

lessons.idea: Snap judgments can be hijacked by appearance.
The difference is whether the cue is actually relevant.
lessons.anchor: Expert thin-slicing versus the Harding error

lessons.idea: Hidden biases show up in who gets chosen.

reflect: When did someone's appearance or confidence mislead you?
Which 'looks right' signals do you trust too much?
reflect_final: In your next quick judgment of a person, what will you check before you trust it?

use_cases.situation: Your team is excited about a candidate who 'looks like a leader'.
use_cases.move: Ask what evidence of the actual skills you've seen, beyond presence and appearance.

use_cases.situation: You're quick to dismiss a quiet colleague's ideas.
use_cases.move: Evaluate the idea on paper, without the name attached.

use_cases.situation: A friend is dazzled by a charming new business partner.
use_cases.move: Ask what track record the partner has, apart from the good impression.

pocket_idea: Looking the part is not the same as being able to do it.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Warren Harding became president partly because he looked like one.

conversation_variants.question_idea: When has looking right fooled you?
